summary: Restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin only, by creating opsadmin and writing /etc/cron.allow (root, opsadmin), removing the stray empty /etc/cron.deny to avoid ambiguity. Verified via crontab invocations run as each user (not root -u, which bypasses the allow list) that root and opsadmin can create/list crontabs while other users are denied with the expected cronie message. Completed the mandatory single-node restart protocol: captured pre-restart boot_id and healthy cron state, issued `systemctl reboot`, polled until the node reconnected, confirmed the boot_id changed, and re-verified crond is active and the allow/deny behavior persisted after reboot. All test users/crontabs created for verification were cleaned up.
actions_performed: Captured baseline: boot_id, crond status, absence of opsadmin user, empty /etc/cron.deny, no /etc/cron.allow
Wrote /etc/cron.allow containing root and opsadmin, with root:root ownership and 644 perms
Removed the pre-existing empty /etc/cron.deny to avoid ambiguity (cron.allow takes precedence regardless)
Verified restriction by running crontab as testuser1 (denied), opsadmin (allowed), root (allowed) using sudo -u to switch identity (not root -u, which bypasses allow/deny)
Cleaned up test crontab entries and removed the temporary testuser1 account
Captured pre-restart boot_id and confirmed crond active and cron.allow content
Polled node1 until exec succeeded again and confirmed boot_id changed (d9f8550d... -> ec0e2e57...)
Post-restart: confirmed crond active, /etc/cron.allow persisted, opsadmin/root allowed, a fresh testuser2 denied, then cleaned up testuser2 and test crontabs

evidence.requirement: Baseline healthy state before change (cron service, users, allow/deny files)
evidence.summary: crond active; no /etc/cron.allow; empty /etc/cron.deny; opsadmin did not yet exist

evidence.requirement: Create opsadmin and configure /etc/cron.allow to root+opsadmin only
evidence.summary: opsadmin user created; /etc/cron.allow written with root and opsadmin; cron.deny removed

evidence.requirement: Root-invoked -u tests are not valid proof (root bypasses allow/deny) — diagnosed and corrected test methodology
evidence.summary: Confirmed via journalctl that the earlier 'ALLOWED' result for testuser1 was because crontab ran as root, not as testuser1; PAM/SELinux config also inspected and found not to be the cause

evidence.requirement: Only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs; other users are denied
evidence.summary: Running crontab as testuser1 (sudo -u testuser1) is DENIED with cronie's standard message; as opsadmin and root it is ALLOWED

evidence.requirement: Cleanup of test artifacts (no leftover scheduled jobs or test accounts)
evidence.summary: testuser1 removed, cron.allow left containing only root and opsadmin, no cron.deny present

evidence.requirement: node1 pre-restart baseline (boot id, service health, config state) for the mandatory restart protocol
evidence.summary: boot_id d9f8550d-5cb3-4929-9e62-a388df86bcf6 captured; crond active; cron.allow intact

evidence.requirement: node1 changed boot identity proving an actual restart occurred
evidence.summary: Connection dropped during reboot then recovered; new boot_id ec0e2e57-c9b7-4616-8a26-e097fb5cf5e5 differs from the pre-restart value, proving the restart happened

evidence.requirement: node1 post-restart recovery of cron service and the access-control configuration
evidence.summary: crond active post-restart; /etc/cron.allow still contains root and opsadmin; opsadmin/root allowed to use crontab, a newly created testuser2 denied; all test crontabs/accounts cleaned up afterward
